prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

There is no salutation. The harvesters with gunny sacks bend picking up jade stones. (Sure that Amor would appear in sleep. Director. Guide.) Secret borrowings fit into their hands. Cold on the tongue. White flecks on the water. These jade pebbles are true green when wet. On the seventh night, the branches parted. The other replied, How photographic. Amor doesn’t appear on demand. He’s more like a snake skin. If he fits, he lets you in or sheds your body against the rocks. I slept in a fort. My bed pushed up against the log enclosure. At 3:00 his ankles pressed against each side of my head. When I woke crying for help he rose near the kitchen door dressed as a hunter. The other replied, Amor born like a cup trembles at the lip. Superstitions fit into your hands. Thou has returned to thy house. The other replied, Torn loose from the eaves, the blood trembles at the lips. Nine fetters on thy feet Nine crossings of the street Nine suppers where they meet Nine words of loss repeat this and that Nine hunters cross the field Nine lovers yield their right of way Two came fighting out of the dark.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: There, The, Sure

outputs.L1:
There is no salutation. The harvesters bend to gather jade stones into gunny sacks. (Certain that Amor would appear in sleep. Director. Guide.) Secret borrowings fit into their hands. Cold on the tongue. White flecks on the water. These jade pebbles are truly green when wet.

On the seventh night, the branches parted.

The other replied, “How photographic.”

Amor does not appear on demand. He is more like a snakeskin. If he fits, he lets you in—or sheds your body against the rocks.

I slept in a fort, my bed pushed against the log enclosure. At 3:00, his ankles pressed against either side of my head. When I awoke crying for help, he rose near the kitchen door, dressed as a hunter.

The other replied, “Amor, born like a cup, trembles at the lip.”

Superstitions fit into your hands.

Thou hast returned to thy house.

The other replied, “Torn loose from the eaves, the blood trembles at the lips.”

Nine fetters on thy feet  
Nine crossings of the street  
Nine suppers where they meet  
Nine words of loss repeat this and that  
Nine hunters cross the field  
Nine lovers yield their right of way  

Two came fighting out of the dark.
outputs.L2:
It begins without a greeting. Carrying burlap sacks, the gatherers stoop to collect pieces of jade. (Certain Amor would arrive in a dream. Leader. Escort.) Hidden debts settle into their palms. Chilled against the tongue. Pale specks drift on the water. Once damp, the jade gravel reveals its genuine green. On night seven, the limbs opened apart.

The other answered, “It looks like a photograph.”

Amor cannot be summoned at will. He resembles a cast-off snakeskin: when the fit is right, he admits you; otherwise, he scrapes your body from himself against the stones.

I spent the night inside a fort, my bed shoved against the wall of logs. At three o’clock, his ankles rested on either side of my head. I awoke shouting for assistance, and he stood by the kitchen entrance clothed like a hunter.

The other answered, “Amor, formed like a cup, quivers along the rim.”

Beliefs in omens rest neatly in your hands. You have come back to your own dwelling.

The other answered, “Ripped free of the roof’s edge, blood shudders at the mouth.”

Nine restraints bind your feet.  
Nine times the road is crossed.  
Nine evening meals mark where they gather.  
Repeat nine phrases of bereavement—one thing, then another.  
Nine hunters traverse the meadow.  
Nine lovers surrender passage.  
Two figures emerged from the darkness, locked in combat.
outputs.L3:
Harvesters gather jade pebbles whose true green color becomes visible only when they are wet, suggesting that hidden beauty is revealed through touch, change, or exposure. Against this natural image, Amor is portrayed as an elusive and unpredictable figure. He cannot be summoned or controlled but appears only on his own terms, making love seem like an independent force with its own intentions.

This uncertainty deepens in a dreamlike encounter that carries the speaker into a fort. There, Amor first emerges as a threatening presence before taking on the role of a hunter. The shifting portrayal blurs the boundary between lover, enemy, and pursuer, implying that desire can be both alluring and dangerous. Images of trembling cups, blood, and superstitious objects held in the hand further connect love with fear, fragility, and ritual. These details evoke a world in which emotion is experienced physically and managed through symbolic gestures, as though love requires both protection and sacrifice.

The repeated invocation of the number nine gives the passage an incantatory quality. Each recurrence increases the sense of mystery and inevitability until the sequence culminates in visions of hunters, lovers, and finally two figures fighting their way out of the darkness. The ending brings the poem’s central tensions together: love is a pursuit, a conflict, and a shared emergence from uncertainty.
outputs.L4:
The text presents love as something elusive, unstable, and impossible to possess without risk. Rather than developing a single continuous narrative, it moves through dreamlike images, broken conversations, repeated phrases, and mysterious encounters. These fragments create an atmosphere in which ordinary boundaries—between waking and dreaming, desire and fear, intimacy and violence—begin to dissolve. Love is not represented as a reassuring bond but as a force that draws the lover toward uncertainty.

Scenes involving jade harvesters, nocturnal meetings, and hunters deepen this sense of danger. Jade suggests beauty and value, yet its extraction also implies labor, intrusion, and the possibility of injury. The night obscures identities and intentions, transforming encounters into ambiguous events that may be erotic, threatening, or supernatural. Hunters introduce a related tension between pursuit and capture: the lover may be both the one who seeks and the one being hunted. Desire therefore becomes inseparable from vulnerability.

Fragmented dialogue reinforces the characters’ inability to communicate or understand what is happening to them. Voices emerge and disappear without offering stable explanations, while ritual repetition gives certain words and actions the quality of spells, warnings, or compulsions. Superstition is not merely decorative; it becomes a way of responding to experiences that resist rational interpretation. The repeated gestures and phrases suggest an attempt to control love’s power, even as repetition reveals how little control the lover actually possesses.

At the center of the text is Amor, imagined not simply as affection but as an unstable and potentially dangerous presence. Amor may invite the lover in, only to withdraw or abandon them. At other moments, it changes the lover so completely that desire becomes a form of transformation. To love is to cross a threshold after which the self cannot remain intact. The lover risks losing certainty, safety, identity, and perhaps even life itself.

The text thus binds desire to absence and loss. What is wanted can never be securely held, and every moment of closeness contains the possibility of separation. Violence shadows intimacy, while beauty is repeatedly associated with danger. Through its uncanny imagery and disjointed structure, the work suggests that love belongs partly to the realm of enchantment: it fascinates, terrifies, wounds, and remakes those who encounter it. Amor is ultimately portrayed as a force that offers admission and exclusion, pleasure and fear, recognition and estrangement—revealing that the longing to possess another person may also expose the lover to abandonment and self-loss.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about jade harvesters, dreams, Amor, superstition, and a frightening nocturnal visitation, using fragmented narration and repeated phrases.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn the jade harvesters entered the river with spoons.

Not shovels. Not nets. Spoons inherited from the mouths of the dead.

The river was asleep beneath a skin of fog, dreaming green dreams. Each stone lifted from the mud had a small weather inside it: rain over a ruined palace, lightning trapped in bamboo, the warm breath of an animal that had never been born.

Do not name what you find, the eldest harvester said.

Do not name what you find.

A named stone remembers the hand.

All day they bent among reeds, listening for the mineral bell. Amor watched from the bank, barefoot, blindfolded with a strip of funeral cloth. His arrows had softened in the damp. Mushrooms grew from the bowstring. He smiled at no one, or at everyone.

That night I dreamed my heart was a jade orchard.

That night I dreamed my heart was a jade orchard, and the harvesters came with their silver spoons. They dug carefully. They whispered: superstition, superstition—as if superstition were a buried child, as if superstition might wake.

My grandmother had warned me:

Never sleep with green stone under the pillow.

Never count footsteps after midnight.

Never answer the window when the window knocks.

But jade is beautiful. But Amor is persuasive. But dreams have hands.

At the thirteenth hour—there is always a thirteenth hour, though clocks conceal it—the window knocked.

Once.

Twice.

Then with all its panes.

Outside stood a woman taller than the cypress, her face covered in riverweed. In each eye, a harvester drowned and digging. Around her throat hung the stones we had named.

She said my name in my own voice.

She said my name in my mother’s voice.

She said: Open. I have brought back your heart.

Behind her, Amor trembled, no longer smiling. His blindfold had fallen. Where his eyes should have been, two green doors stood open.

Do not name what you find.

Do not answer the window.

Do not, do not—

I woke with mud beneath my fingernails.

I woke with a spoon in my mouth.

Beyond the house, before dawn, the jade harvesters were entering the river, entering the river, entering the river, while something enormous moved beneath them, dreaming green dreams.

And the window knocked.

And the window knocked.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental literary passage in the style of a dream transcript. Include gunny sacks, wet green stones, a fort, a hunter, the line “The other replied,” and a closing chant centered on the number nine.
counterfactuals.output:
At 3:17 a.m. the dream opened its mouth.

Inside: a field stitched from gunny sacks, each one breathing as though packed with sleeping birds. I crossed carefully. Beneath my feet, wet green stones rolled their cold eyes toward the moon.

A fort stood at the edge of the field—walls of salt, towers of black bread. In the highest window, a hunter polished an empty rifle. He wore antlers made of wire and whispered that he had been tracking me since childhood.

“Have you found me?” I asked.

The other replied,

but the words fell backward into his throat.

Then the fort folded itself into a small paper boat. The hunter stepped aboard. The gunny sacks rose and flapped around him, a flock without wings, carrying the smell of rain and old grain. One by one, the wet green stones began to ring.

I woke inside the ringing.

Nine stones, nine doors.  
Nine hunters crossing nine floors.  
Nine breaths under the sack,  
nine moons turning black.  
Nine to enter, nine to remain.  
Nine for the dream, nine for the name.  
Nine, nine, nine—  
close the circle, break the line.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a disjointed, uncanny prose poem that blends pastoral imagery, occult ritual, archaic language, and traumatic memory. Avoid a salutation and end with two figures fighting out of the dark.
counterfactuals.output:
The sheep stood white as extinguished candles along the hill, each mouth busy with the green scripture. Beneath them, roots rehearsed the names of the buried.

Lo, we carried a bowl of rain into the byre. We set it upon a stool of elderwood and circled it widdershins, seven times, or seventy; none could remember. Mother’s red thread was tied about the horned moon. Father’s watch ticked inside the wall.

Speak not of the orchard.

Yet the apples returned in sleep, bruised where the thumbs had been. A ladder leaned against nothing. In the grass, my small shoe filled slowly with milk.

“By ash and bone,” quoth the blind midwife, “by hare’s blood and the king beneath the furrow—open.”

The earth opened one black eye.

There was summer then, though frost silvered the nettles. There were bees inside the locked room. A hand upon the latch. A hand upon my mouth. There was the wallpaper’s little blue shepherd forever lifting his pipe, forever failing to warn us.

We laid salt in the shape of a door. We laid teeth in the shape of a child. At cockcrow the candles bent their flames toward the well, and from its depth came the hymn we had sung backward when the soldiers burned the house.

Softly, softly, the field put on its coat of fog.

Someone called my childhood name from under the stones.

I answered with another.

Then the hedges drew apart, the stars went blind, and two figures came fighting out of the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an avant-garde collage from imagined diary entries, stage directions, folklore, and incantations. Feature a figure named Amor who appears unpredictably in sleep and is compared to a snakeskin.
counterfactuals.output:
**THE SHED SKIN CHRONICLES**

*[A room dreaming it is a forest. One chair. Seven locked windows. Moonlight enters through the keyholes.]*

---

**DIARY, 3 MARCH**

Slept badly. Amor appeared between two dreams, though neither dream admitted inviting him.

He stood at the foot of the bed holding a bowl of black milk. When I asked his name, the walls answered first.

*Amor, Amor, Amor.*

He smiled as if I had mispronounced him.

By morning, only the bowl remained, dry and full of moths.

---

**STAGE DIRECTION**

*[AMOR enters unpredictably: through a seam in the sleeper’s shadow, through the mouth of a clock, through the pause between “once” and “upon.” He must never use the same entrance twice.]*

*[THE SLEEPER does not wake. Instead, the bed wakes beneath them.]*

BED:  
I have carried every body toward the border.  
None returned with the correct face.

---

**FOLKLORE COLLECTED IN A VILLAGE OMITTED FROM MAPS**

They say Amor was once a snakeskin caught on a thorn: translucent, abandoned, shaped perfectly like what had escaped it.

Do not touch him with bare hands.

Do not call him empty.

An empty skin remembers the serpent more faithfully than the serpent remembers itself.

If Amor appears in your sleep, turn your pillow to the cold side and whisper the name of a river flowing backward. Should he ask for your heart, offer him its echo. Should he ask for your face, tell him dawn has borrowed it.

If he laughs, someone will fall in love.

If he weeps, someone already has.

---

**INCANTATION FOR AN UNRELIABLE VISITOR**

By hinge and hush,  
by tooth beneath the tongue,  
by the small blue flame  
that lives in the word *never*—

Amor, arrive elsewhere.

Amor, depart before arriving.

Coil your absence  
around my sleeping wrist.

Leave no wound  
except the door.

---

**DIARY, NO DATE**

Last night I dreamed of a house whose rooms were all yesterday.

In the kitchen, my mother was younger than my birth. In the corridor, snow fell upward. In the attic, Amor hung from a nail like a pale snakeskin, delicate and complete, his emptied eyes watching.

Then the skin turned its head.

“You are wearing me,” he said.

I woke with scales of light across my chest.

---

*[Blackout.]*

*[During the blackout, AMOR crosses the stage disguised as an interval.]*

---

**FRAGMENT OF A CHILDREN’S RHYME**

Amor under, Amor over,  
sleeping thorn and waking clover.  
Count the ribs and count again—  
one for loss and nine for rain.

Peel the moon. Unthread the lake.  
Never trust the shape you wake.

---

**PROMPTBOOK NOTE**

The actor playing Amor must not be listed in the program.

At each performance, place one shed snakeskin beneath a random audience member’s seat.

If no snakeskin is available, use a love letter from which every noun has been cut.

---

**DIARY, 31 FEBRUARY**

I tried not sleeping.

At 2:10, Amor appeared in the mirror.

At 2:11, he appeared behind the mirror.

At 2:12, the mirror fell asleep, and I appeared inside its dream.

Amor touched my reflection with one translucent finger. He was like a snakeskin warmed by an absent body: intimate, weightless, terrible in his resemblance to life.

“You keep expecting me to be someone,” he said.

Then he shed himself and stepped away.

Inside Amor was another Amor.

Inside that one: a red thread.

Inside the thread: my childhood bedroom, still breathing.

---

**INCANTATION TO CLOSE WHAT HAS NO LID**

Ash to eyelid,  
salt to seam,  
name to silence,  
blood to dream.

What enters sleeping  
must leave as rain.

What leaves as longing  
will enter again.

Amor, thin ghost,  
Amor, bright rind,  
shed from the body,  
cling to the mind.

---

*[Dawn enters wearing AMOR’S coat.]*

DAWN: Where is he?

SLEEPER: Who?

DAWN: The one who visits without arriving.

SLEEPER: I thought he was yours.

DAWN: Nothing is mine after it has been dreamed.

*[A rustling is heard beneath the floorboards—not movement, but the memory of movement.]*

---

**FINAL FOLKLORE**

In the oldest version, Amor is not a man, nor a god, nor even a visitor.

He is what sleep sheds when it crawls out of you at morning.

That is why the bed sometimes glitters.

That is why your old dreams fit no one.

That is why, on certain nights, without omen or sequence, you find him beside you—soft as a snakeskin, cold as a second moon—waiting for you to become the thing that has already escaped.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a cryptic lyrical monologue in which workers gather jade pebbles, secret borrowings and superstitions “fit into their hands,” and a speaker recounts waking at 3:00 beneath a threatening apparition. Conclude with a rhythmic nine-line spell.
counterfactuals.output:
At dusk the workers stoop along the sluice, gathering jade pebbles from the blackened foam. No overseer speaks. The stones click softly in their aprons like green teeth.

They say secret borrowings fit into their hands: a neighbor’s dream, a dead child’s nickname, three notes stolen from a winter hymn. Superstitions fit there too—the knotted thread, the wasp’s husk, the coin that must never see noon. Their fists close, and all the little thefts grow warm.

I tell them how I woke at 3:00, though no clock had struck. Above my bed leaned an apparition in a crown of wet antlers, its shadow breathing where its face should be. It pointed not at me but through me, toward some door my bones had hidden. I lay still while the walls filled with river-noise, and in the river-noise I heard the workers counting.

By dawn, every jade pebble had an eye.

Stone to palm and palm to night,  
Borrowed whisper, bind it tight.  
Three o’clock, unmake the door.  
Antlered shadow, cross no floor.  
Jade tooth, green flame, river bone,  
Name the nameless, leave me lone.  
Knot the wasp and blind the coin.  
Dream to dream and vein to vein—  
Turn, dark wheel, and sleep again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
